this was the film that really helped me out a ton when I first started doing production design- watching interviews with Sam Lisenco (the p.d) introduced me to a new world of film production, and I'm forever thankful for it. finally, after some years, I've come around to see the film that had a huge impact on my aspiring career and deepened my understanding and appreciation of film as a whole. it's a given that what makes this film feel very special is the world and setting of this middle school, the use of intertextuality, and fantastic direction from the character acting, the specific style of cinematography, and the outstanding art direction. This is a very charming coming-of-age story that feels very magical for its modern and internet-age depiction of middle school. I was going into my senior year of high school when this came out, but youth-hood is a timeless experience all the same. In all honesty it would be unfair to compare this to a show like PEN15 because of its lack of social commentary, yes obviously they are both coming of age stories with awkward and anxious preteens, but both pieces of media are accomplishing two different goals. PEN15 has its two female leads, Maya and Anna, who bring a lot of interesting dialogue to be said about race and class in television. Usually I would label a film like this as “white people: the movie” but it would rub me the wrong way doing so as such, so I’ll make a one time exception for this film.

"Growing up can be a little bit scary and weird." — Kayla Day Eighth Grade follows a young person who struggles to express themselves and turns to internet video to build self-confidence. Bo Burnham is recognised for his realistic depiction of the internet, effectively illustrating what motivates people to create content. He presents the internet as a space for self-expression, reflection, and performance, often without an audience, particularly in unwatched vlogs. To ensure authenticity, Burnham cast real eighth graders and addressed mature topics relevant to their age group. The MPAA assigned the film an R rating, which sparked controversy by restricting access for actual eighth graders. In response, A24 organised free, unrated screenings across the United States. This film serves as Generation Z's counterpart to "Thirteen" (2003), though "Thirteen" used lighting to convey its darker themes. In Eighth Grade, students are often absorbed in their phones. Modern mean girls rarely make direct, passive-aggressive remarks, since that would require personal interaction. Instead, they exclude others by ignoring those they consider uncool. While this behaviour is harsh, the film does not portray these popular students as villains. Instead, it shows them coping with their own insecurities. Ultimately, there are no villains in Eighth Grade; the characters are young people trying to understand themselves and their lives. I would love to see another film that is both an interesting social commentary for teens and a generally good film with deep emotional ties that people can relate to.

Spending hours trying to engineer the perfect Instagram post like it might somehow engineer a better version of yourself. Every Snapchat story felt like evidence in the case for whether or not you of all people were worth noticing. Eighth Grade understands that before you know who you are, you're already performing as someone else. Every hallway feels like an audience. The boys are impossibly dreamy, the girls impossibly cruel, your parents impossibly embarrassing, and adulthood seems like the cure for it, a glimmer of hope through it all. What a beautiful tragedy it is to be thirteen; how special it is that a movie can almost let us do it all over again.

Wanted to cry for most of this movie. Did cry at several scenes. I love her dad. His monologues are unbelievable. I adore Bo Burnham and his screenwriting. It's incredible how he goes from viscerally cringe dialogue to randomly inserting these subtly beautiful, understated lines. "It's dumb in a way that it's fun to play when it's raining outside" stood out to me for this reason. There's something to be said about how this movie does not use gratuitous violence. I knew what was coming from having shadowed my colleague's film class when this was being covered, but the "bad" scenes still made me nauseous and unsettled. I kept awaiting an escalation, as other popular films have conditioned me to anticipate, and yet the escalation never came. I like that Bo Burnham rejects the spectacle of violence in this respect. Culturally and artistically, we've overly normalized the use of unnecessary violence and brutality in the arts. I'm talking specifically about violence that isn't necessary to plot development. Violence in this respect is used to replace screen-writing that is a) legitimately good and b) trusts the audience's intelligence by instead choosing to depict implied violence. Sure, media literacy is abysmal nowadays, but that's no reason to make art that essentially hinges on the audience's willingness to actively participate in the degradation and oppression of vulnerable, marginalized people (which, for the record, many of the "greats" necessitate we do). Incredibly symptomatic of its time, almost like a time capsule. Missing Bo Burnham's screenwriting a little extra today. Great work.

i don't think anyone will ever understand what this film means to me. i watched it for the first time at 17, when i had already grown out of my preteen awkward phase and somehow considered myself at that point to be a full-fledged adult. but as i watch this film again as a girl in my mid-20s, this stirred something in me i didn’t expect. when i was 17 i saw my younger self in kayla. awkward, anxious, always wanting to be chosen, too shy to talk to the cool kids, and feeling so uncomfortable in my own skin. but at that time of viewing the movie, all i could think was, “thank god that phase is over.” and yes, most of us do not miss that age. but now at 25, i found myself crying with love for this character. that version of ourselves that feels so overdramatic and inexperienced and terrified of growing up, who only a couple of years prior to puberty couldn’t care less if other kids thought she was cool enough. kayla stares at her 6th grade time capsule, addressed on the front “to the coolest girl in the world.” she somehow is depressed and embarrassed that her 11 year old self had that much confidence that her older self would be just that. but it’s that exact kind of confidence that allows us to not only stop judging the awkward versions of ourselves, but to embrace them with our whole hearts. every phase of life is a stepping stone to the next, but every version of ourselves is a part of us. be kind to every age you find yourself in, and cherish it. you grow every day from who you were yesterday, but you don’t forget that awkward girl that got you to where you are today. bo burnham i adore you so much. thank you for this film
